{
  "question_intent": "Earnings-call question on BUK product margin, ISA season impact, cards seasonality, day count, USCB business pricing pressure",
  "main_topics": ["BUK product margin", "ISA season impact", "cards seasonality", "day count", "USCB business pricing pressure"],
  "answer_completeness": "Complete",
  "response_stance": "Direct",
  "evidence_level": "High",
  "contains_numeric_evidence": true,
  "contains_forward_guidance": false,
  "narrative_alignment": "Aligned",
  "question_quote": "Morning Anna, Sachin Nayar from Goldman Sachs. First question, just on the BUK product margin. So I think there was around a £50 million headwind at Q1, primarily from the roll-off of five year [Covid] mortgages and then £61 million at Q2, so slightly higher than expected. You mentioned on the call a larger and more competitive ISA season and now you expect a neutral to positive impact for H2. So could you just elaborate on some of the assumptions there? I think you mentioned in spite of competitive deposit pricing, there is an impact from cards seasonality and day count, could you maybe quantify those or even talk about the moving parts going forward through to even 2027 if possible? And then secondly, just on the USCB business, I guess following up from Amit's question, on the pricing pressure to non-NII, what proportion of the business roughly is impacted by this, given of course Best Egg is an originate to distribute model. Are some of those numbers you gave earlier, such as the $700 million revenue uplift per annum, are those still relevant now or should we maybe lower our expectations slightly? Thank you.",
  "answer_quote": "Let me start and I refer to some of this in my prepared remarks, but me go back to it. So we guided at Q1 that we would expect the margin impact to be broadly similar in Q2 and it goes from like £52 [million] to £61 [million], so it's marginally worse. That number of £61 [million] is somewhat exaggerated by the fact that we grew the structural hedge in absolute terms, the notional at the back end of Q1. So what that means is we are moving income out of the product margin and into the structural hedge bucket. So those two numbers are inflated and somewhat exaggerate the effects. Now that's a couple of times we've called that out. Clearly, we've had a more stable structural hedge notional in Q2, so you're not going to see that impact in Q3. Secondly, you called out mortgages. So just to remind everybody, we have this cohort of mortgages from 2021, written during the stamp duty holiday in Covid at wide margins, that is rolling off. [It is] an industry wide matter and a substantive proportion of it has rolled off thus far. Then for deposits, you are right, the deposit margins or the deposit market was a bit more competitive than we expected. But let me just take you back to the numbers. We said it would be broadly stable and we're talking about a number here, that's £61 [million] versus £52 [million]. So it was marginally worse than we anticipated and that's just because the market was very buoyant, 7% growth year on year. This churn within the time deposits market, we were able to somewhat step back, because most of our maturities were in Q1 and not Q2. So that allowed us to really focus on that Premier brand, which is what we did. As I look forward into Q3 and Q4, there are many fewer maturities of those time deposits and we know what those market maturities are. The second thing is, you are now seeing a situation where the front book and the back book margins are somewhat converging and the pricing didn't change from here, they would be neutral by the fourth quarter. So the pricing pressure in volume and margin terms in deposits is dissipating as the year continues. Then the last thing is, you just see stronger cards seasonality towards the back end of the year. We've seen pretty good underlying growth, but towards the end of the year, you just see higher level of purchases naturally. It's not as extreme as the US, but it is there, so you're going to see that. Then there's day count. There are just more days in the second half than there are in the first. I'll let you guys work that out and work out what the impact of it is, so I'm not going to call out a number, but equally that does help. That's why Q1 is always a [lower print]. [On USCB], look, the non-NII and Best Egg, the only pressure on non-NII is coming from Best Egg and it's coming from the point that I called out, which is these securitisation margins. I still think the $700 million is a relevant number. What we are saying is that it would just take us a bit longer to grow back to that Q1 base and to the extent that reference rates move around, you will see that margin move around a little bit and it's just because, if you imagine you are the purchaser of those loans, the reference rate matters because you are raising wholesale funding to buy them. So to the extent that the reference rate is going up and the APR is not, it just creates a bit of margin pressure on their sales, that's all we're seeing. It's a bit of margin compression, nothing significant. And as I said before, we have mechanisms to be able to modify that in time either by holding a bit more on the balance sheet, or alternatively by controlling the placing of those securitisations more fully ourselves. So we have some optionality here and we'll talk about that more in time, but you will have heard some of our peers, with similar businesses call out exactly the same impact [in Q2].",
  "reason": "The response provides a direct answer to the question with high evidence level, including numeric evidence and a clear narrative alignment with the question's intent. It addresses the main topics and contains a complete answer with a forward guidance statement."
}
